title: Large unconditional cash transfers improved reported parenting while increasing some reported child stress signals
source_unit: U.S. families in a randomized three-year unconditional-cash-transfer experiment, with child, parenting, care, and household outcomes

observations.period: Three-year transfer experiment; NBER Working Paper issued July 2025 and revised February 2026

denominator.unit: randomized study frame; abstract does not state one pooled respondent denominator

transfer_contrast.unit: monthly randomized assignment for three years

child_expenditures.unit: reported treatment direction for monthly spending on children

reported_child_developmental_difficultie.unit: reported treatment direction; authors note possible connection to closer monitoring

lowest_income_parenting_and_nonparental_.value: largest parenting improvements; increased use and quality of non-parental childcare

null_outcomes.value: no meaningful effect on most administrative educational outcomes, home-environment characteristics, child food security, homelessness exposure, or parental satisfaction

mobility.value: families were more likely to move, with no detected change in most neighborhood-quality measures

observations.method: NBER Working Paper 34040 studies a large randomized unconditional cash transfer of $1,000 per month for three years versus $50 per month and examines parenting, child investment, developmental outcomes, care, housing, and family wellbeing.
observations.uncertainty: This record retains the official abstract-level findings rather than reproduced coefficients, sample construction, attrition, measurement instruments, or full robustness results. The reported child-developmental-difficulty result may reflect increased observation from closer monitoring; it is not by itself a clinical deterioration estimate.
observations.subgroup: Families in the randomized study, with reported largest parenting improvements among those with the lowest baseline incomes.
observations.counterinterpretation: More spending, supervision, and non-parental childcare can coexist with more reported child difficulty or stress and no change in parental satisfaction. A transfer can improve some care inputs without producing uniform wellbeing or educational gains.

related_sources.claim: NBER DOI and working-paper metadata identify the study and authors.

boundary: This is a randomized U.S. transfer-to-parenting and care result, not a universal cash-transfer effect or a complete child-development, household-welfare, employment, trust, political-action, or long-run recovery estimate.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: Official NBER Working Paper 34040 page downloaded and hashed; title, date, randomized transfer contrast, parenting, child-stress, care, mobility, subgroup, and null-outcome findings checked against the abstract.
